problem.summary: Detectors trained on fixed predefined category sets cannot handle open-vocabulary real-world scenes, while existing open-vocabulary detectors rely on heavy vision-language fusion or distillation that inflates inference latency and hinders deployment.
statements: Detectors trained on predefined categories are limited in real-world scenarios with an open vocabulary.
Prior open-vocabulary methods distill VLM predictions or add deep image-language fusion modules, which suffer from high inference latency.
Even the first real-time open-vocabulary detector loses speed because of its text-image fusion module.

evidence.quote: Traditional object detection methods are typically trained on a set of predefined categories, which limits the application in real-world scenarios with open vocabulary.
However, these methods suffers from high inference lantency.
the text-image fusion module still results in a reduction of the inference speed.

background.summary: The report builds directly on the authors' LW-DETR real-time DETR baseline and on CLIP-style vision-language pretraining, positioning prior open-vocabulary detectors (distillation-based, deep-fusion, and YOLO-World) as accurate but slow or fusion-dependent.

evidence.quote: However, the computation deployment consumption continue to pose challenges for the practical application of ov-detector in real-world scenarios.
The key of open-vocabulary detection is on transferring the language knowledge in VLM to object detector.

solution.summary: OVLW-DETR transfers vision-language knowledge into the LW-DETR detector by swapping the detector's fixed classification weights (and the fixed weights of the mixed-query top-K spatial selection) for class-name embeddings produced by a frozen CLIP text encoder, keeping the architecture unchanged and free of fusion modules.
solution.approach: Replace fixed classification-layer and query-selection weights in a light-weight DETR with class-name text embeddings from a frozen VLM text encoder, enabling open-vocabulary classification by simple alignment.
components: LW-DETR detector (ViT encoder, projector, DETR decoder)
frozen text encoder taken from a pretrained VLM (CLIP ConvNeXt-Large)
class-name text embeddings replacing the fixed classification layer weights
text embeddings also replacing fixed weights in top-K spatial query selection
IA-BCE loss and Group DETR parallel weight-sharing decoders retained for training
detector fine-tuned for 12 epochs while the text encoder stays frozen

evidence.quote: We align detector with the text encoder from VLM by replacing the fixed classification layer weights in detector with the classname embeddings extracted from the text encoder.
Open-vocabulary classification is enabled by simple alignment between detector and VLM text encoder, modifying the the mixed-query selection scheme and classification layer.
The fixed layer weights in both selecting top-K spatial queries scheme and query classification layers are replaced with the text embedding extracted by the text encoder.
Without additional fusion module, the model retains its inherent architecture, thereby enhancing its flexibility and facilitating a more efficient deployment.

experiments.summary: The S/M/L variants initialized from LW-DETR are fine-tuned on GoldG and Objects365 with a frozen CLIP text encoder and evaluated zero-shot on LVIS v1.0 minival (1203 categories), reporting AP, rare/common/frequent AP, parameter count and T4 latency against GLIPv2 and YOLO-World/YOLO-Worldv2.

evidence.quote: OVLW-DETR achieves or outperforms on zero-shot LVIS minival benchmark on different scales.
Without multi-modal fusion module, OVLW-DETR maintains the low latency in inference while also demonstrating impressive performance.

limitations.summary: The report states no limitations explicitly; evident constraints are that evaluation is confined to a single zero-shot benchmark and the text encoder is frozen throughout training so it cannot adapt to detection data.
items: No dedicated limitations section in the report.
Evaluation is reported only on LVIS v1.0 minival, one zero-shot benchmark.
The text encoder is frozen during training, so language features are never fine-tuned on detection data.
Only S/M/L variants inherited from LW-DETR are considered.

evidence.quote: We use LVIS v1.0 minivalKamath et al. [2021] as benchmark since this dataset contains 1203 categories, with a long tail of rare categories.
We fine-tune the pre-trained detector on standard LW-DETR training receipt, while the text encoder is frozen during training process to retain the generalization ability.

applications.detail: The report frames open vocabulary as required because detectors restricted to predefined categories cannot serve real-world deployments.
applications.quote: which limits the application in real-world scenarios with open vocabulary

applications.detail: Computation and deployment cost of open-vocabulary detectors is identified as a barrier to practical application.
applications.quote: However, the computation deployment consumption continue to pose challenges for the practical application of ov-detector in real-world scenarios.

deploymentClaims: Described as a deployment-friendly open-vocabulary detector with strong performance and low latency.
No additional fusion module keeps the model easier to implement and modulate for deployment.
OVLW-DETR-S measures 3.23 ms latency versus 5.58 ms for YOLO-Worldv2-S on a T4 GPU with FP16.

evidence.quote: Without additional fusing module, OVLW-DETR is flexible and deployment friendly, making it easier to implement and modulate.
We measure the averaged inference latency in an end-to-end manner with fp16 precision and a batch size of 1 on LVIS v1 minival on one T4 GPU, with 1203 categories.
